newsitem.title: PUERTO RICO: Puerto Rico Gov proposes $18 bln budget for FY98.
newsitem.headline: Puerto Rico Gov proposes $18 bln budget for FY98.

text.p: Puerto Rico Gov. Pedro Rossello unveiled an $18.04 billion budget for fiscal year 1998, marking an increase of 3.1 percent, the smallest budget hike on this U.S. commonwealth in three years.
Targeting what he called "the five fingers of a decisive hand," Rossello detailed a budget focused on public safety, health, education, housing and job creation.

Public safety is slated to get $1.4 billion, up from the $1.2 billion the sector received under the current budget. Included in the new budget is more money for the police, corrections and fire departments.
"This budget and this action speaks for itself of our committment to recover peace," Rossello said in a Tuesday evening speech to the Legislature.
Puerto Rico has been hit over the past decade with a wave of drug-related violence. Its homicide rate is one of the highest under the U.S. flag.
Rossello, who was first elected in 1992 and re-elected in 1996, promised an "iron fist" against crime. He has increased spending on public safety by about 65 percent since 1993.

Also slated for an increase by Rossello is education, which will receive $2.07 billion up from the current $1.9 billion. Housing will receive $526 million, up from $473 million, and health services are slated to receive $2.27 billion, up from $2.25 billion.
"The health of our people for you, likely ,is more than just a committment," Rossello told the island's lawmakers. "It's a sacred obligation."

Under Rossello, who is a pediatrician, Puerto Rico's government has launched a health care reform that provides managed care services to the indigent. Nearly two-thirds of the island's population receives public aid of some sort and its per capita income trails behind U.S. states.

The government on this Spanish-speaking island receives most of its revenue from its so-called General Fund, which includes tax revenues and accounts for approximately 32 percent of the government's income.

Another 30 percent comes from revenue earned by the island's publicly owned corporations, such as its telephone company, its electric power authority and its water utility. Federal funds account for 18 percent of revenues.

Rossello said total government revenue increased at least 30 percent from 1993 to 1997. For fiscal 1998, which begins July 1, the General Fund is expected to increase from $5.62 billion to $6.01 billion. Rossello attributed the increase to more business being created and higher tax revenues.

Puerto Rico recently phased in tax reform that slashed corporate and individual rates in an attempt to encourage more people to file returns. The island's government has also aggresively pursued individuals and companies who owe back taxes.
Rossello's budget was presented to the legislature, which will now debate, modify and vote on the proposal. Puerto Rico has a constitutionally madated balanced budget.
